summary: Children aged 7-9 learn to distinguish two different motions of Earth on two different timescales: the daily SPIN on its axis (~24 hours, causing day and night) and the yearly ORBIT around the Sun (~365 days, one year). The load-bearing idea is that day/night is caused by us rotating into and out of sunlight, NOT by the Sun moving, switching off, or being covered by clouds. Teach kinaesthetically first (child or globe spinning beside a fixed lamp), separate the two motions before combining them, and always name which motion produces which effect over what period.
misconceptions: Thinking day and night are caused by the Sun moving around a stationary Earth, or by the Sun switching off/being covered by clouds, rather than by Earth's rotation.
Confusing rotation with revolution — believing one spin takes a year, or that the orbit causes day and night.
Believing the Earth's orbit (distance from the Sun) causes day and night, or later, seasons — conflating the two motions and their effects.
Thinking the whole Earth is dark at night (not grasping that it is always daytime somewhere — the opposite side).
Assuming the Sun physically rises and sets by moving, not realising the apparent motion is produced by our own rotation.

activities.title: Spin into night: the globe and the fixed lamp
steps: In a darkened room, set up a single fixed light source (a lamp) as the Sun; it must not move.
Hold or stand a globe beside the lamp and stick a marker on your home town.
Slowly spin the globe and watch your marked town travel from the lit side (day) into the shadow side (night) and back again — one full turn = one day.
Describe out loud what is moving: say whether the Sun or the globe is turning.
Find and point to the terminator — the sharp line where day meets night on the globe.
activities.insight: Day and night happen because Earth spins and our side turns to face or away from a Sun that stays put; it is always daytime somewhere on the other side.

activities.title: Two journeys, two clocks: separate spin from orbit
steps: First, practise only the spin: turn the globe one full rotation and name it 'one day, about 24 hours'.
Next, draw an orbit path on the floor with the Sun (lamp) at the centre.

Keep the globe spinning while you walk it all the way around the Sun; one full lap = one year, about 365 days. Remember that the real Earth spins about 365 times during one lap, far more than you can turn the globe while walking.
Say aloud which motion gives day/night (the spin) and which gives the year (the orbit).
Connect 365 days to the calendar year you already know.
activities.insight: Rotation (spin) and revolution (orbit) are two different motions on two very different timescales: one spin makes a day, one orbit makes a year. The orbit does NOT cause day and night.

activities.title: Two views at once: the spin and the rising Sun
steps: Watch, or model, the spinning Earth from the outside (a space view) at the same time as a ground view where the Sun appears to rise, cross the sky, and set.
As your home-town marker spins toward the light, notice the Sun 'rising'; as it spins away, notice the Sun 'setting'.
Say the click-moment aloud: 'It's not the Sun moving — it's me turning away from it.'

Test the old idea: try moving the Sun around a still Earth and notice that, from the ground, the Sun still seems to rise and set. Discuss how the spinning-Earth model gives the same sky, and that scientists know Earth really spins from other evidence, not from the sunrise view alone.
activities.insight: The Sun's apparent rise and set across the sky is produced by our own rotation; linking the real spin to the apparent Sun movement helps replace the geocentric intuition.

activities.title: Explore the lit hemisphere from any angle
steps: Using a 3D model or by moving around a spinning globe, view the lit hemisphere from different angles.
Fly or walk to the terminator and look along the day/night boundary.
Travel to the far (night) side and confirm it is dark while the near side is in day.
Explain why it is always day somewhere on Earth at the same time.
activities.insight: The Earth-Sun system is spatial: viewing the lit hemisphere from any angle makes it clear that day and night exist simultaneously on opposite sides of a spinning Earth.

activities.title: Check and sort: motion, effect, timescale
steps: Match each motion to its effect and its timescale: spin → day/night → ~24 hours; orbit → year → ~365 days.
Put the parts of a day in order as a spot rotates through dawn, noon, dusk, and midnight.
Answer a question that confronts the 'Sun moves' idea by choosing and justifying what really happens.
Explain in your own words why the orbit does not cause day and night.
activities.insight: After building the motion intuition, learners can recall and apply the two facts and reject the common misconceptions.

checkQuestion: What makes it change from day to night and back again — is it the Sun travelling across and around the Earth, is it the Earth going all the way around the Sun each day, or is it something else? Tell me what really happens, and WHY it gives us day and night.
checkAnswer: Day and night happen because the Earth SPINS (rotates) on its axis once about every 24 hours. As it turns, the side facing the Sun has day and the side turned away has night. The Sun doesn't actually travel around us — it only LOOKS like it moves across the sky because we are the ones turning. Earth ALSO travels around the Sun, but that much slower journey takes a whole year (365 days) and gives us the year, not day and night.
